explanation: 802.11ac is Wi-Fi 5 and operates only in the 5 GHz band, which is why it reaches higher rates than 802.11n but has shorter range and fewer legacy clients. 2.4 GHz support in a Wi-Fi 5 access point comes from a separate 802.11n radio.

choices.text: 5 GHz only, marketed as Wi-Fi 5
2.4 GHz only, marketed as Wi-Fi 5
Both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz, marketed as Wi-Fi 4
6 GHz only, marketed as Wi-Fi 6E

stem: Which amendment is marketed as Wi-Fi 7 and introduces multi-link operation?
explanation: 802.11be is Wi-Fi 7. Multi-link operation lets a client use more than one band with the same access point at the same time, and 320 MHz channels widen the pipe further. It builds on the 6 GHz support that Wi-Fi 6E already added.

stem: Which IPv6 prefix contains the global unicast addresses that are routable on the internet?
explanation: 2000::/3 covers the global unicast space that IANA allocates to the registries, which in turn assign blocks to providers and enterprises. FE80::/10 is link-local and never routed, FC00::/7 is unique local, and FF00::/8 is multicast.

stem: Which IPv6 multicast address does a host join so that neighbour solicitation for its address reaches it?
explanation: The solicited-node multicast address is FF02::1:FF00:0/104 with the low 24 bits of the target address appended. A node joins it for every address it configures, so neighbour solicitation is delivered only to hosts whose addresses could match instead of to the whole link.

choices.text: The solicited-node multicast address built from the low 24 bits of the target address
FF02::1, the all-nodes multicast address
FF02::2, the all-routers multicast address
The all-nodes address of the link-local prefix

stem: During duplicate address detection, which source address does a host use while it verifies that its tentative address is unique?
explanation: The host has not yet been allowed to use the tentative address, so it sends the neighbour solicitation from the unspecified address ::. If no neighbour advertisement comes back, it can assign the address. Using the tentative address as the source would defeat the purpose of the check.

choices.text: The unspecified address, ::
The loopback address, ::1
The tentative address being tested
The link-local address of the default gateway

stem: In a spine-leaf fabric, which switch connects the fabric to the WAN, firewalls, and load balancers?
explanation: Spines exist only to move traffic between leaves, so all off-fabric connectivity is placed on border leafs. That keeps the spine tier uniform and puts routing policy, security zones, and external peering at a defined edge point.

choices.text: A border leaf
A spine switch
A core switch in the campus block
An out-of-band management switch

stem: A leaf has 48 ports at 25 Gbps toward servers and four 100 Gbps uplinks to the spines. What does the resulting oversubscription ratio describe?
explanation: Oversubscription compares the bandwidth offered by the downstream ports with the bandwidth available upstream. Here 48 x 25 Gbps is 1.2 Tbps against 400 Gbps of uplink, a 3:1 ratio, which assumes servers will not all demand line rate at once. A lower ratio costs more but reduces contention.

choices.text: The ratio of downstream server bandwidth to upstream uplink bandwidth, here 3:1
The number of spines a single leaf can join at once
The number of MAC addresses the leaf can hold in its table
The ratio of control-plane traffic to data-plane traffic on the spine

stem: How is each link between a leaf and a spine addressed in a routed spine-leaf fabric?
explanation: Every leaf-to-spine link is its own point-to-point subnet, commonly a /31, so each link is a separate Layer 3 hop with no shared broadcast domain. That is what allows equal-cost multipathing over all spines and removes spanning tree from the fabric.

choices.text: As a dedicated point-to-point IP subnet, often a /31, with the leaf and spine as its two endpoints
As part of one large VLAN shared by every leaf and spine
With no IP address at all, since the link only switches frames
From a single management subnet assigned to all fabric ports

stem: An interface must support at least 1,000 hosts. Which prefix length gives the smallest subnet that still satisfies the requirement?
explanation: Work backwards from the host count: 2^10 - 2 = 1,022 usable addresses, which is the first power of two at or above 1,000. Ten host bits means a /22. A /21 would waste 1,022 addresses, and a /23 with only 510 usable hosts falls short.

stem: Which address is a valid host address inside the subnet 192.168.44.0/26?
explanation: A /26 has a block size of 64, so 192.168.44.0/26 spans .0 through .63. The .0 address names the subnet and .63 is its broadcast, leaving .1 through .62 for hosts. The address .64 belongs to the next subnet and is itself a network address.

stem: In a server farm behind a load balancer, clients are configured with one address that the balancer owns rather than a server address. What is that address called?
explanation: Clients send to the virtual IP and the balancer rewrites the destination, or the source in some modes, to a chosen pool member. That indirection is what lets servers be added, drained, or replaced without reconfiguring a single client.

choices.text: A virtual IP address (VIP)
A loopback address configured on every pool member
A DHCP relay address for the server subnet
A floating static route shared by the servers

stem: Why is the spanning-tree root bridge normally placed on a core or distribution switch instead of an access switch?
explanation: Root placement decides which links get blocked. Put the root in the middle of the topology and the blocked ports land where redundancy is cheapest, between access switches, instead of cutting a core uplink that every VLAN depends on. A root stranded at the edge stretches the tree across the whole campus.

choices.text: Because the root sits at the topological centre, so blocked links fall on redundant access paths rather than core links
Because only core and distribution switches run spanning tree
Because access switches cannot be configured as root bridges
Because root placement determines which VLANs an access switch is allowed to carry

stem: What distinguishes multimode fiber from single-mode fiber in a campus backbone?
explanation: Multimode has a wide core that lets several propagation modes travel at once, which suits building and campus runs of a few hundred metres with cheaper optics. Single-mode has a tiny core that carries one mode, holding signal integrity over kilometres but needing costlier laser transceivers.

choices.text: Multimode carries several light paths over shorter, cheaper links; single-mode carries one path over long distances
Multimode uses laser transceivers while single-mode uses LEDs
Multimode is immune to electromagnetic interference while single-mode is not
Multimode caps out at 100 Mb/s while single-mode supports 10 Gb/s

stem: A TCP sender receives three duplicate ACKs for the same sequence number. What does fast retransmit do?
explanation: Duplicate ACKs tell the sender that everything after the gap arrived. Three of them is strong enough evidence of loss that the sender resends the missing segment immediately, then halves the window and continues in fast recovery rather than waiting for a retransmission timer or restarting from slow start.

choices.text: Retransmits the missing segment at once without waiting for the retransmission timer
Halves the congestion window and restarts from slow start
Tears down the connection and reopens it
Retransmits every unacknowledged segment in the window

stem: An IPv6 router decrements a packet's Hop Limit to zero. What does the router do with that packet?
explanation: Hop Limit is the IPv6 equivalent of TTL: hitting zero means the packet has looped or the path is longer than allowed, so the router drops it and reports ICMPv6 Time Exceeded to the source. Traceroute builds on exactly that response.

choices.text: Discards it and returns ICMPv6 Time Exceeded to the source
Forwards it with the Hop Limit reset to 1
Fragments it and rewrites the Hop Limit
Holds it in a queue until a shorter path becomes available

stem: A frame crosses a router on its way to a remote network. Which part of the original PDU does the router discard and rebuild before forwarding?
explanation: A router strips the incoming Layer 2 header and trailer, then builds a new frame header for the outgoing link. The IP packet itself is forwarded unchanged apart from the TTL decrement and header checksum.

choices.text: The data-link frame header and trailer
The IP header
The transport-layer header
The application payload

stem: What is the broadcast address of the subnet that contains the host address 172.20.131.200/21?
explanation: A /21 mask leaves five host bits in the third octet, so subnets step in blocks of eight. 131 falls inside 128-135, which makes 172.20.135.255 the directed broadcast.

stem: A host is configured with the IPv6 address 2001:db8:1:2::a1b2:c3d4. Which solicited-node multicast address does the host join for that address?
explanation: The solicited-node address is ff02::1:ff followed by the low-order 24 bits of the unicast address. The last 32 bits are a1b2c3d4, so the final 24 bits are b2:c3d4.

choices.text: ff02::1:ffb2:c3d4
ff02::1:ffa1:b2c3

stem: A Windows workstation reports the IPv4 address 169.254.37.14 with a mask of 255.255.0.0. What does that address tell a troubleshooter?
explanation: 169.254.0.0/16 is the link-local range a Windows host self-assigns when it cannot reach a DHCP server. The address works only on the local segment and signals a DHCP reachability problem.

choices.text: The host could not reach a DHCP server and self-assigned a link-local address
The host received a valid lease from a DHCP scope in the 169.254.0.0/16 range
The host is using a manually configured RFC 1918 private address
The host has been assigned a loopback alias by the operating system

stem: Why is Category 6A specified instead of Category 6 for a 10GBASE-T run that must reach the full 100-meter channel?
explanation: Category 6A is characterised to 500 MHz and adds alien-crosstalk control that Category 6 lacks, which is what allows 10GBASE-T to reach 100 meters rather than the roughly 55 meters Category 6 supports.

choices.text: Cat 6A is characterised to 500 MHz and controls alien crosstalk, so it carries 10GBASE-T for 100 m
Cat 6A uses a different pinout that doubles the usable pairs
Cat 6A is shielded, which lets it exceed the 100-meter channel limit
Cat 6A is the only category rated for 40GBASE-T at 100 m

stem: In a cloud VPC, how does a security group differ from a network ACL?
explanation: A security group is stateful and attaches to an instance network interface with allow-only rules. A network ACL is stateless, applies at the subnet boundary, and supports both allow and deny statements.

A security group is stateless and applied to a subnet, while a NACL is stateful and attached to an instance

Both are stateless, but only a security group can contain allow rules

stem: Which statement best explains why a container starts in under a second while a virtual machine needs far longer?
explanation: A container shares the host kernel and carries only the application plus its user-space libraries, so there is no guest operating system to boot. A virtual machine boots a full OS image.

choices.text: A container shares the host kernel and packages only the application and its user-space dependencies

A container keeps its filesystem in RAM instead of on disk
A container uses hardware passthrough to skip the boot process

stem: Why does 802.11 use carrier sense multiple access with collision avoidance rather than the collision detection used on wired Ethernet?
explanation: A radio cannot listen for a collision on the same channel while it is transmitting, so collisions can only be avoided rather than detected. 802.11 relies on random backoff, optional RTS/CTS, and positive acknowledgements.

choices.text: A wireless station cannot reliably transmit and listen for collisions on the same channel at once
Wireless frames are too small for collision detection circuitry to resolve
802.11 has no acknowledgements, so collisions must be prevented entirely
The access point assigns every station a dedicated time slot with no contention

stem: A provider sells an MPLS Layer 3 VPN to two customers that both use 10.0.0.0/8 internally. How does the provider keep the overlapping prefixes separate?
explanation: Each customer is bound to its own VRF with a private routing table, and route targets control which prefixes are imported into each VRF. Overlapping addresses therefore never share a forwarding table.

choices.text: Each customer is bound to a separate VRF and route targets control which prefixes are imported
The provider translates both customers into a shared public addressing range
Each customer receives a unique autonomous system number that overrides the overlap
The provider relies on longest-prefix match to distinguish two identical 10.0.0.0/8 advertisements

stem: A stateful firewall drops the return packets of a connection it permitted outbound. Forward and return paths are known to traverse different firewalls. What explains the drop?
explanation: A stateful firewall only permits return traffic that matches an existing session in its own state table. If the reply arrives at a different firewall that never saw the outbound flow, no session exists and the packet is dropped.

choices.text: The returning packets reach a firewall that never observed the outbound flow, so no session exists to match
The firewall ACL is applied in the wrong direction on the inside interface
The connection uses UDP, which stateful inspection cannot track
The firewall NAT pool has been exhausted by earlier sessions

stem: A monitoring host that opens thousands of short-lived HTTP connections to a controller eventually fails new connections with 'Cannot assign requested address'. Which resource is exhausted?
explanation: Each outbound connection consumes an ephemeral source port. Sockets lingering in TIME_WAIT hold their four-tuple, so a high churn of short connections exhausts the local ephemeral port range.

choices.text: The ephemeral source port range, held by sockets in TIME_WAIT
The TCP receive window advertised by the controller
The local ARP cache entry limit
The interface maximum transmission unit

stem: Why do campus designs deliberately limit the size of a single Layer 2 domain?
explanation: Broadcast and unknown-unicast flooding, MAC table size, and the blast radius of a spanning-tree topology change all grow with the Layer 2 domain. Routing between smaller domains contains those effects.

choices.text: Flooding volume and spanning-tree convergence scope grow with the size of the domain

A large Layer 2 domain prevents the use of 802.1Q trunks between switches
MAC addresses must be unique inside a Layer 2 domain and cannot be reused elsewhere

stem: Two switches are joined by a duplex fiber patch cord, but neither interface comes up. Both transceivers are compatible and powered. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Fiber is directional: each strand carries traffic one way. If transmit is cabled to transmit on both ends, neither receiver ever sees light and the link stays down.

choices.text: The transmit strand at one end is connected to the transmit strand at the other end
The fiber cable is too short for the transceiver to lock onto the signal
The two interfaces are configured with different duplex settings
The SFP modules must both come from the same vendor

stem: An IPv4 header carries an IHL field with the value 15. How long is that header?
explanation: The IHL field counts 32-bit words, not bytes. A value of 15 therefore means 15 times 4, or 60 bytes, which is the maximum an IPv4 header can be once options are included.

choices.text: 60 bytes

40 bytes
64 bytes

stem: What does the Total Length field of an IPv4 header measure?
explanation: Total Length covers the header and the payload together, so a full 1500-byte Ethernet payload reports 1500. Subtracting the IHL-derived header size leaves the actual data length.

choices.text: The header plus the payload, in bytes
Only the payload, in bytes
Only the header, in 32-bit words
The number of routers the packet may still cross

stem: Which IPv4 header field lets a destination group fragments that belong to the same original packet?
explanation: Every fragment of one datagram carries the same Identification value, and the fragment offset then positions it. Together the two fields allow correct reassembly even when fragments arrive out of order.

choices.text: Identification
Total Length
Header Checksum
Protocol

stem: How is the upper-layer protocol identified in an IPv6 packet that carries extension headers?
explanation: Each extension header ends with its own Next Header field, so the value chains forward header by header. The final Next Header value in the chain names the transport protocol or ICMPv6.

A fixed field in the base header always names it, whatever extensions follow

The Payload Length encodes the protocol number

stem: Why does a routed spine-leaf fabric not need spanning tree across the data center?
explanation: Each leaf-to-spine link is its own point-to-point IP subnet, so there is no Layer 2 loop to block. Every uplink can carry traffic at once, and equal-cost multipath spreads flows across them.

choices.text: Every leaf-to-spine link is a routed point-to-point subnet, so no Layer 2 loop exists

Leaves connect to only one spine at a time, which removes any loop
Servers handle loop prevention in software before sending frames

stem: Why is eBGP commonly chosen as the routing protocol between leaves and spines in a large fabric?
explanation: A per-link eBGP session with a unique ASN per switch gives loop-free paths without flooding link state across the whole fabric, and it scales to thousands of nodes while supporting multipath.

choices.text: Unique ASNs per switch give loop-free paths with no fabric-wide link-state flooding and easy multipath

stem: Why does a spine-leaf fabric use spine ports only for fabric uplinks and never for servers?
explanation: Leaving servers off the spines keeps each spine a pure transit tier whose full port count adds bisectional bandwidth. Capacity grows by adding spines, and leaves absorb all server attachment.

choices.text: Keeping spines as pure transit lets every spine port add fabric bandwidth, and growth comes from adding spines

stem: What does a mobility group provide in a multi-controller wireless deployment?
explanation: Controllers in the same mobility group share client context over mobility tunnels, so a client that roams to an AP on another controller keeps its session and does not re-authenticate.

choices.text: It shares client context between controllers so roaming clients keep their sessions
It load-balances CAPWAP control traffic across the wireless management VLAN
It synchronises the WLC configuration database between controllers
It assigns radio channels and transmit power to access points

stem: What does an access point do when it is placed in monitor mode?
explanation: A monitor-mode AP stops serving clients and dedicates its radio to passively capturing frames for intrusion detection and site surveys. It is a sensor, not an access point for users.

choices.text: It stops serving clients and passively captures wireless traffic for analysis
It serves clients but forwards their traffic locally instead of to the controller
It becomes a backup controller for the APs in its mobility group
It converts its radio to a dedicated backhaul link between buildings

stem: Ping replies to a remote site are fast, but large file transfers to that site crawl. No interface shows errors and the link is not saturated. What best explains the throughput?
explanation: A TCP sender may have only one window in flight per round trip, so throughput is capped near window size divided by RTT. Long paths therefore need a larger window to fill the link, even when latency looks fine to a ping.

choices.text: Throughput is limited by the TCP window divided by the round-trip time
The path MTU is smaller than the server's interface MTU, so every frame is dropped
The remote site's DNS server is answering slowly
The client NIC is negotiating half duplex with the access switch

stem: Users report strong Wi-Fi signal but slow throughput, and the problem worsens as more people join the same area. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Signal strength says nothing about airtime. When many clients share one channel they contend for the same medium, so each station waits longer and aggregate throughput per client falls.

choices.text: Clients on the same channel are contending for airtime
The AP transmit power is too low for the coverage area
The clients are receiving addresses from the wrong DHCP scope
The SSID is hidden, so clients must probe more often

stem: Which combination of amendment and spectrum defines Wi-Fi 6E?
explanation: Wi-Fi 6E is 802.11ax operating in the newly opened 6 GHz band. The PHY is the same as Wi-Fi 6; the E denotes the additional spectrum, which supplies many more non-overlapping channels.

choices.text: 802.11ax extended into the 6 GHz band
802.11ac extended into the 6 GHz band
802.11be restricted to the 5 GHz band
802.11n extended into the 60 GHz band

stem: Which modulation scheme did 802.11ac introduce that 802.11n does not use?
explanation: 802.11ac added 256-QAM, carrying eight bits per subcarrier instead of the six of 64-QAM. The denser constellation demands a better signal-to-noise ratio to stay decodable.

choices.text: 256-QAM
64-QAM
DSSS with Barker coding
Binary phase-shift keying

stem: What is the widest channel 802.11n can use?
explanation: 802.11n introduced channel bonding but caps it at two 20 MHz channels, giving 40 MHz. Wider 80 and 160 MHz channels only arrived with 802.11ac.

choices.text: 40 MHz
20 MHz
80 MHz
160 MHz

stem: What is the maximum channel length for a twisted-pair Ethernet link such as 100BASE-TX or 1000BASE-T?
explanation: The 100-meter channel budget covers up to 90 m of permanently installed horizontal cable plus 10 m of patch cords at each end. Exceeding it causes attenuation and crosstalk failures that show up as CRC errors.

choices.text: 100 meters
90 meters
500 meters
185 meters

stem: Which fiber medium is required to carry 10GBASE-ER across its full 40-kilometer reach?
explanation: 10GBASE-ER uses 1550 nm optics over single-mode fiber to reach 40 km. Multimode grades lose too much signal over that distance, so OM1 or OM3 would fall far short.

choices.text: Single-mode fiber
OM1 multimode fiber
OM3 multimode fiber
Category 6A twisted pair

stem: How many equal /27 subnets can be carved out of the address block 10.0.0.0/24?
explanation: A /27 borrows three host bits from a /24, and two to the third power is eight. Each resulting subnet holds 32 addresses, 30 of which are usable.

stem: Which prefix length provides exactly 62 usable host addresses on a subnet?
explanation: A /26 leaves six host bits, so the block contains 64 addresses. Subtracting the network and broadcast addresses leaves 62 usable hosts.

stem: In a conventional /64 IPv6 subnet, how many bits make up the interface identifier?
explanation: A /64 splits the 128-bit address in half: the first 64 bits are the subnet prefix and the remaining 64 bits identify the interface. That width is what makes stateless address autoconfiguration practical.

stem: Which IPv6 prefix is reserved for use in documentation and examples?
explanation: RFC 3849 sets aside 2001:db8::/32 for documentation so examples never collide with real global unicast space. Lab topologies and textbooks use it for exactly that reason.

stem: At which OSI layer does a repeater or hub operate?
explanation: A repeater regenerates the electrical signal without reading addresses or headers, so it works purely at the physical layer. That is why a hub extends a collision domain rather than dividing it.

choices.text: Physical
Data link
Network
Transport

stem: Which two OSI layers correspond to the network access layer of the TCP/IP model?
explanation: The TCP/IP network access layer covers everything below IP, so it absorbs the OSI data-link and physical layers. The internet layer maps to OSI network, and the transport layer stays one-to-one.

choices.text: Data link and physical
Network and transport
Session and presentation
Transport and application

stem: What is the role of a CSU/DSU on a legacy serial WAN circuit?
explanation: The channel service unit terminates the provider's digital line and the data service unit converts between line signalling and the router's serial interface. Modern handoffs usually fold both functions into the provider demarcation device.

choices.text: It terminates the digital carrier circuit and presents a serial interface to the router
It converts copper Ethernet to fiber
It load-balances traffic across two circuits
It encrypts traffic before it enters the provider network

stem: What does a service level agreement on a business WAN circuit typically guarantee?
explanation: An SLA is a contractual performance envelope covering uptime, one-way delay, delay variation, and time to repair. Pricing and CPE management are separate commercial terms.

choices.text: Availability, latency, jitter, and repair time targets
A fixed monthly price for all bandwidth upgrades
That the provider will manage the customer's routers
Unlimited bandwidth with no committed rate

stem: What does a virtual machine snapshot capture?
explanation: A snapshot records the current disk, and optionally memory, so the VM can be reverted to that instant. It is not a backup, because it normally lives on the same storage as the running VM.

choices.text: The VM's disk and memory state at a point in time for rollback
A full backup copy stored on a remote tape library
A container image exported for reuse on another host
A copy of the hypervisor's global configuration only

stem: Why do multiple containers built from the same image use less disk space than the equivalent number of virtual machines?
explanation: Container images are stacked read-only layers that many containers can share, with a thin writable layer on top. Virtual machines each carry a complete guest operating system image.

choices.text: Their read-only image layers are shared and only the writable layer is unique
Containers compress their filesystems automatically at runtime
Containers store their data in RAM instead of on disk
Each container mounts the host filesystem read-only

stem: What does a reverse proxy placed in front of web servers provide?
explanation: A reverse proxy is the public face of a service: clients connect to it and it relays requests to one or more backends. That hides server topology and centralizes TLS, caching, and request filtering.

choices.text: It accepts client requests and forwards them to backend servers, hiding the servers and often terminating TLS
It caches DNS answers for internal clients
It assigns addresses to guests on the wireless LAN
It inspects outbound traffic from internal users

stem: What does a network access control deployment check before admitting a device to the network?
explanation: NAC combines authentication with a posture check, so a known device running outdated antivirus or missing patches can be quarantined. Admission depends on both who the device is and what state it is in.

choices.text: The device's identity and its compliance with policy such as patch level or endpoint protection
The device's routing table for a usable default route
The speed of the switch port the device is plugged into
Whether the device already holds a DHCP reservation
